Roadmap: from an inherited database to control and value

Source: vignettes/articles/roadmap.Rmd
roadmap.Rmd

You have inherited a large database: several schemas, hundreds of tables, tens of thousands of columns, no documentation, and reports that disagree with each other. This article sets out the order of work from there to a database that is under control and useful to the business, which stages DBinventory covers, and what each stage needs from people rather than code.

It revises the original plan (“From 700 undocumented tables to the first semantic model”), which named eleven artefacts in five stages. The artefacts stand; what has changed is that the first two exist, the key work has started, and the sequence can now be stated as questions the business is asking, in the order they can be answered.

Three principles

Triage, do not document. Most of the tables are copies of each other at different levels of aggregation. Documentation effort goes only to the small canonical set, once it is known. Nothing is described by hand at scale.

Generate, then review. Profiles, duplicate clusters, candidate keys and first-draft descriptions can all be produced by code. A person reviews before anything carries a “reviewed” flag; nothing is asserted on the strength of a heuristic alone.

Record provenance, not rival definitions. Where a metric has several definitions in use, the register records each as observed (where, by whom, what it computes, when). Making disagreement visible and attributable is what people are asking for when they ask for numbers that agree.

The sequence

Each phase shrinks the problem for the next: profiling shows which tables are copies, deduplication shows which deserve documentation, documentation states grain and keys, and the key register is what a semantic model is built from.

Phase Question it answers Artefacts (original numbering) Done by Gate to the next phase
0. Access and safety Can we look without risk? Read-only account; a home for outputs that holds no patient data Code (built: value suppression is the default) Outputs reviewed as safe to commit
1. Know what exists What is there, how big, how fresh, what is empty? 1 Inventory, 2 Column profile Code (built: inventory_run()) Every table and column profiled; failures explained
2. Collapse to the canonical set Which 5 to 10 per cent of tables are the real sources? 3 Duplicate and lineage map, 4 Naming and classification standard Code proposes clusters; warehouse owners confirm Canonical list agreed with the owners
3. Keys and structure What is one row of each canonical table, and how do they join? 8 Key register, 7 Conceptual entity model Code tests candidates (started: pk_candidate, fk_candidate); people decide Every canonical table has a reviewed grain and a tested key; core joins pass
4. Document the canonical set What does each table and term mean? 5 Data dictionary, 6 Business glossary Drafted from the profile, reviewed by people; glossary anchored to the NHS Data Dictionary Dictionary rows marked reviewed; glossary covers the first metrics’ terms
5. Control Who owns what, what is tested, how do definitions change? 10 Data quality baseline, 11 Stewardship and change control, 9 Metric definition register Tests in code on a schedule; named stewards; register kept by the team A steward per canonical table; tests green; first metrics registered with provenance
6. Value Can the business answer its own questions from certified data? Semantic model (entities from 7, relationships from 8, metrics from 9, descriptions from 5 and 6); decommissioning of the duplicates Modeller, with the registers as input Certified datasets in use; duplicate tables retired

Phase 0: access and safety

A read-only login with SELECT on the objects is enough; INFORMATION_SCHEMA is readable without system views or Query Store. The outputs of phase 1 are committed to a repository, so they must not carry patient data: the profile withholds literal values for identifiers, free text and personal-data column names by default, and the review of that output is the first gate.

Phase 1: know what exists

One run of inventory_run() against the warehouse gives every table and column with row counts, sizes, the newest datetime per table, and a profile of every column. This is the only phase that is purely mechanical, and it already answers questions the business asks: which tables are stale, which are empty, where the volume is, which columns hold personal data. Expect the first run to fail on a few objects (broken views, permissions); the run log says which, and the run resumes rather than restarts.

Phase 2: collapse to the canonical set

Columns with the same value fingerprint across tables are the same data stored again. Clustering tables by shared fingerprints, then picking the widest, freshest, lowest-grain member of each cluster with the fewest project-specific filters, is the work that turns hundreds of tables into tens. The candidate duplicate columns in the report are the seed; the next piece of code clusters whole tables and proposes a canonical member with a rationale. The classification standard (source, reference, derived, scratch; canonical, duplicate, deprecated; sensitivity classes) is written during this phase, because the categories only become clear from the data. This is also the first phase that needs the warehouse owners in the room: the canonical list is an assertion about which copy is right, and they know things the profile cannot show.

Phase 3: keys and structure

The profile already marks primary key candidates and proposes foreign keys from names, value sets, ranges and cardinality. Those are shortlists. The key register confirms them with match-rate tests (what share of a child’s values exist in the key) on the canonical set only, and records uniqueness, nulls and whether a key survives across normalisation levels. The dm package does this confirmation and then holds the result as a data model with an entity relationship diagram, so the register should be built on it rather than reimplemented. The conceptual entity model is deliberately small and independent of tables: the dozen things the hospital counts and how they nest. Grain, stated as “one row is one what”, is the single most important field, because every later decision about additivity and fan-out depends on it.

Phase 4: document the canonical set

The data dictionary covers canonical tables only. Descriptions are drafted from the profile (name, type, sample values, neighbouring columns) and carry a status per row so drafted and reviewed text are never confused; the file shape borrows from the Open Data Contract Standard so it converts outward later. The glossary is separate from the dictionary because a term such as “referral” is carried by many columns and its meaning is a business matter: where a national definition exists in the NHS Data Dictionary, cite it and record the local deviation.

Phase 5: control

Control is three things, none of them large: automated tests on the canonical set (key uniqueness, referential integrity, freshness, row-count drift) run on a schedule with results logged; a named steward for each canonical table and glossary term, with a page saying how a change is proposed and logged; and the metric register, which records each definition as observed with provenance and never asserts a correct answer. The register is the artefact most likely to meet resistance, so its design matters: two definitions sit side by side with where each was seen.

Phase 6: value

With the gates passed, the semantic model is mechanical: entities from the conceptual model, relationships from the key register, dimensions and descriptions from the dictionary, metrics from the register. Which engine compiles it is an implementation choice for then. The other half of the value is subtraction: the hundreds of duplicate tables can be retired with confidence, because the canonical set is known, tested and owned.

What DBinventory does and what comes next

Built: phases 0 and 1 in full (inventory, profile, suppression, resumable store, exports, report), and the shortlist half of phase 3 (pk_candidate, fk_candidate with evidence and confidence).

Next, in order:

  1. Table clustering for phase 2: cluster tables by shared fingerprints, classify each member (copy, aggregate, filtered subset, wider derivative, unknown), propose a canonical member with a rationale, and emit the list for the owners to confirm.
  2. Key register for phase 3: confirm the shortlisted keys with match-rate tests, through dm, and record the results per entity.
  3. Incremental re-profiling: re-run only tables whose row count or newest datetime has changed, so the inventory can run on a schedule.
  4. Dictionary drafts for phase 4: a first-draft description per canonical column from the profile, with a status field, in the ODCS shape.

Phases 5 and 6 are mostly people and pages rather than package features; the package’s job there is to keep the inventory and tests current so that what the stewards sign off stays true.

Ready to start semantic modelling when

  • A canonical table exists for every core entity and is agreed with the warehouse owners.
  • Every canonical table has a reviewed grain and a tested primary key.
  • Joins between core entities are in the key register with passing referential tests.
  • The glossary covers the terms the first metrics will use.
  • The metric register holds at least the first few metrics with provenance.
  • Someone is named as steward for each canonical table.
